subtitle: A summary and index of the one hundred RFCs numbered 3400 through 3499 with brief descriptions of each.

tldr.problem: The RFC series grows rapidly and readers need a way to understand what the recent RFCs cover and find the ones relevant to their work.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 3499 is an annotated index listing all RFCs from 3400 to 3499, with a title, brief description, and status track notation for each to help readers navigate the RFC series.
tldr.outcome: This periodic summary document serves as a snapshot of the standards published during a 100-RFC window, making it easier for engineers and protocol developers to discover relevant specifications.

today: RFC 3499 is an Informational index document that summarizes the RFCs published in the 3400-3499 range. It is not a technical standard and has not been obsoleted. While the status information it contains is from December 2003, it remains a useful historical reference for understanding what protocols and specifications were published during that period.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope
sections.content:
RFC 3499 is a periodic summary document published by the RFC Editor that indexes and describes the 100 RFCs numbered from 3400 through 3499. Each RFC in this range is listed with its number, title, author(s), publication date, and a brief description of its content. The document is informational, not a technical specification.

The purpose of such summary documents is to help the Internet community navigate the rapidly growing RFC series by providing a convenient reference for the RFCs published in a particular numbering range. This allows researchers, implementers, and engineers to quickly discover relevant protocols and standards without having to search individual RFC documents.
sections.eli5: Someone at the RFC Editor's office created a guide to 100 RFC documents, telling you in a few lines what each one is about.

sections.title: Topics Covered
sections.content: The RFCs in the 3400-3499 range span a wide variety of Internet technologies and applications. Notable areas include: MPLS (Multiprotocol Label Switching) signaling and operations, IPv6 support (including socket API extensions and address selection), internationalization of domain names (IDNA), SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) extensions for instant messaging and compression, network management MIBs for SONET and ADSL, cryptography standards (PKCS #1), media gateway control protocols, mail system extensions (including delivery status notifications), and content delivery networking. Some RFCs on standards track are noted with [STANDARDS TRACK] to indicate they are in the standards-track process.
sections.eli5: These hundred documents cover a huge range of topics: how routers talk to each other, how computers find websites, how video and phone calls work online, and many other networking and internet technologies.

sections.title: How to Use This Document
sections.content:
To find an RFC in this range, readers can scan the alphabetically or numerically organized list to locate RFCs of interest. Each entry includes the RFC number, author name(s), publication date, and a one- to four-sentence description of the RFC's purpose and scope. For RFCs that are part of the standards-track process, a [STANDARDS TRACK] notation is appended.

The document header notes that the status of standards-track RFCs may change over time, so readers should consult the latest edition of "Internet Official Protocol Standards" (also known as RFC 2026-bis or similar current standards status documents) for the most up-to-date status of any RFC listed here. Since this is RFC 3499 from December 2003, readers should verify the current status of any RFC they intend to use.
sections.eli5: You can look through this list, find an RFC number you are interested in, read its short description, and then go find the full document. The guide tells you if it is an official standard or just informational.

sections.title: Standards Track Notation
sections.content:
RFCs in the 3400-3499 range have different status levels within the standards-track process and other categories. Many are Proposed Standards, Draft Standards, or Internet Standards, indicated by [STANDARDS TRACK] in the list. Others are Informational, Experimental, or Best Current Practices documents, indicated by their nature in the description.

The [STANDARDS TRACK] notation does not reflect the RFC's current status but rather notes that it is part of the standards-track process at the time of publication. Standards-track RFCs progress through the Proposed Standard and Draft Standard levels before reaching Internet Standard status. Readers should consult the "Internet Official Protocol Standards" publication for the latest designation of any RFC.
sections.eli5: Some of these RFCs are official standards that the whole internet community agrees to follow. Others are suggestions, experiments, or just information. This guide tells you which is which.
